intro: Combinatorial game theory studies two-player, perfect-information, no-chance games where players alternate moves and the last player unable to move (or, in the 'misere' variant, the last player TO move) loses. The two foundational tools for competitive programming are the Nim game and its XOR-based winning condition, and the Sprague-Grundy theorem, which lets you reduce ANY impartial game (and sums of independent impartial games) to an equivalent single Nim pile via a recursively-defined Grundy number. Together they turn a huge family of 'who wins under optimal play' problems into a mechanical computation.

subtopics.theory:
In standard Nim, there are several piles of stones; on each turn a player chooses one nonempty pile and removes any positive number of stones from it; the player who removes the last stone (equivalently, the player who faces all-empty piles on their turn and cannot move) loses under normal play convention. The celebrated Bouton's theorem states that a Nim position with pile sizes p1, p2, ..., pk is a LOSING position for the player about to move (a 'P-position') if and only if p1 XOR p2 XOR ... XOR pk = 0; otherwise it is a WINNING position ('N-position') for the player about to move. The intuition: from any position with nonzero XOR, there is always a move that zeroes the XOR (reduce whichever pile has the highest differing bit down to the right size), and from any position with zero XOR, EVERY move strictly changes exactly one pile and therefore makes the XOR nonzero again — so zero-XOR positions are exactly the ones from which every move hands the opponent a nonzero-XOR (winning) position, and the all-zero position (immediate loss) has XOR 0, anchoring the induction.

Many contest problems are 'Nim in disguise': the state decomposes into independent components whose sizes you must first compute correctly before XOR-ing them. Staircase Nim is the classic example — balls sit on stairs numbered 1..n, and a legal move takes any positive number of balls from stair k (k != 1) down to stair k-1; the player who cannot move (all balls sit on stair 1) loses. The key insight is that moving balls onto EVEN-numbered stairs is always 'reversible' by the opponent (they can immediately move the same balls one stair further down), so only the balls sitting on ODD-numbered stairs matter strategically — the game is exactly equivalent to ordinary Nim played on the odd-stair ball-counts alone, and you XOR only those.

The misere (last-player-to-move LOSES) variant of Nim has a famously subtle winning condition, distinct from normal Nim except in one common case. Misere Nim's rule: if at least one pile has 2 or more stones, the winning condition is IDENTICAL to normal Nim (XOR of all piles != 0 means the player to move wins) — the extra flexibility of large piles lets the player about to move always steer the game into the normal-Nim endgame in their favor. But if EVERY pile has size 0 or 1 (so the whole game is forced, move by move, with no choice except which pile to touch), the winning condition flips: the player about to move wins if and only if the number of piles with exactly 1 stone is EVEN (because the game becomes purely a parity race to avoid being forced to take the very last stone).

Recognizing when a problem is 'really Nim' is a skill in itself: look for a game with independent piles/heaps, moves that only ever shrink one component, and a normal-play losing condition (can't move = lose); if the removal rule is the unrestricted 'take any positive amount', it's literally Nim and you just XOR pile sizes; if the removal rule is restricted or the piles interact through some structural rule (like the staircase), you first need to find the right transformation or independent decomposition before XOR-ing.
subtopics.recognition: Look for: (a) multiple independent heaps/piles where each move only shrinks one pile and the last player to move wins (normal play) — compute XOR of pile sizes directly; (b) a structural transformation is hinted (stairs, ranges of consecutive integers, etc.) that reduces to an XOR of some derived quantity; (c) explicit mention that the LAST player to move LOSES (misere convention) — check the special all-piles-<=1 case separately from the general XOR rule.
subtopics.complexity: O(n) to compute and XOR all pile sizes (or derived quantities) for a single query; O(1) additional space beyond the input.

examples.title: Classic Nim — Determine the Winner
examples.problem: There are n piles of stones (1 <= n <= 10^5), the i-th pile containing a[i] stones (1 <= a[i] <= 10^9). Two players alternate turns; on each turn a player chooses a nonempty pile and removes any positive number of stones from it. The player who cannot move (all piles are empty) loses. Both players play optimally. Determine who wins: print "First" if the first player wins, otherwise print "Second".
examples.approach: By Bouton's theorem, compute the XOR of all pile sizes. If the XOR is nonzero, the position is an N-position and the first player (about to move) can force a win; if the XOR is zero, the position is a P-position and the second player wins no matter what the first player does.

examples.title: Staircase Nim
examples.problem: There are n stairs, numbered 1 to n, and stair i initially holds b[i] balls (0 <= b[i] <= 10^9). On each turn, a player chooses a stair k with 2 <= k <= n that currently holds at least one ball, and moves any positive number of balls from stair k down to stair k-1 (balls that land on stair 1 are effectively removed from play, since stair 1 cannot be moved from). The player who cannot move (every ball is on stair 1) loses. Determine the winner under optimal play: print "First" or "Second".
examples.approach: This is Staircase Nim: only the ball counts on ODD-numbered stairs (1, 3, 5, ...) matter, because any ball moved onto an even stair can always be immediately mirrored one step further down by the opponent, neutralizing that move; effectively the game reduces to ordinary Nim played on b[1], b[3], b[5], .... Compute the XOR of b[i] for all odd i from 1 to n; the first player wins iff this XOR is nonzero.

examples.title: Misere Nim
examples.problem: There are n piles of stones (1 <= n <= 10^5, 0 <= a[i] <= 10^9). Two players alternate turns; on each turn a player chooses a nonempty pile and removes any positive number of stones from it. Unlike standard Nim, here the player who removes the LAST stone LOSES (misere convention). Both players play optimally. Print "First" if the first player wins, otherwise print "Second".
examples.approach: If at least one pile has 2 or more stones, misere Nim has the SAME winning condition as normal Nim: compute the XOR of all pile sizes, and the first player wins iff it is nonzero. If every pile has size 0 or 1, the outcome instead depends purely on parity: count the piles with exactly 1 stone, and the first player wins iff that count is EVEN (with an even number of forced single-stone moves remaining, the second player is forced to take the last stone).

subtopics.name: Sprague-Grundy Theorem for Composite and Custom Games
subtopics.theory:
The Sprague-Grundy theorem is the master tool that generalizes Nim to ANY impartial game (a game where both players have exactly the same set of legal moves available from any given position, and the last player unable to move loses under normal play). It assigns every position of every impartial game a single non-negative integer, the Grundy number (or 'nimber'), defined recursively as g(position) = mex({ g(position') : position' is reachable from position by one legal move }), where mex (minimum excludant) of a set of non-negative integers is the smallest non-negative integer NOT contained in that set — for example mex({0,1,3}) = 2, mex({1,2}) = 0, and mex(empty set) = 0. A position with g = 0 is exactly a losing position (P-position) for the player about to move; any position with g > 0 is winning (N-position). This recursive definition is a direct generalization of a single Nim pile of size n, whose Grundy number is simply n (since from a pile of n stones you can move to a pile of any size 0..n-1, so mex({0,1,...,n-1}) = n).

The reason mex is the exactly-right operation (rather than, say, max+1 or min) is that it produces the unique value that makes the RESULTING structure behave exactly like a Nim pile of that size: from a position with Grundy number g, you can move to positions with Grundy number EXACTLY 0, 1, ..., g-1 (by definition of mex, all of these must be achievable, or mex would be smaller) but you can also potentially reach positions with other Grundy values >= g or duplicated values — what matters is only that all of 0..g-1 are reachable and g itself is not. This exactly mirrors what a Nim pile of size g can do, which is why the two games are strategically equivalent.

The theorem's real power appears when you combine independent games: if a composite position consists of several independent subgames played simultaneously (a move consists of choosing ONE subgame and making a legal move in it, leaving the others untouched, and the player who cannot move in ANY subgame loses), the Grundy number of the whole composite position is the XOR of the Grundy numbers of the individual subgames — exactly the same combination rule as Nim piles, because Nim itself is just the special case where every subgame IS a simple pile. This lets you decompose a complicated game into independent pieces, compute each piece's Grundy number in isolation (often via a recursive DP with memoization, or by spotting a closed-form/periodic pattern), and then combine everything by XOR.

In practice, computing Grundy numbers for a 'custom' game follows a template: identify the state space (often just a pile size n, sometimes richer), identify which states are terminal (no moves = Grundy 0 by definition, mex of empty set), and compute g[n] bottom-up as the mex of g[n'] over every state n' reachable by one legal move from n. When a single move can SPLIT a position into two or more independent pieces (like splitting a heap of coins into two heaps, à la Grundy's Game), each resulting piece contributes its own Grundy number and you XOR those together before taking the mex over all possible splits — this is the Sprague-Grundy composition rule applied one level down inside the recursive definition itself.
subtopics.recognition: Look for: (a) an impartial game (both players have identical move options everywhere) whose move rule is NOT simply 'remove any positive amount' (so plain Nim doesn't directly apply) — you need to compute a custom Grundy function via mex; (b) a single move that SPLITS a state into two or more independent sub-states (heap splitting, tree/graph decomposition) — combine sub-results via XOR before taking mex; (c) several independent games or piles of DIFFERENT types played as one composite game — compute each type's Grundy function separately, then XOR across all components to get the overall verdict.
subtopics.complexity: Computing a Grundy table g[0..N] for a single-parameter game is typically O(N * M) where M is the number of possible moves/splits considered per state (often O(N) itself, giving O(N^2)); combining k independent components by XOR is O(k) once each component's Grundy number is known.

examples.title: Grundy's Game — Heap Splitting
examples.problem: You are given m independent heaps of coins, the i-th heap having n_i coins (1 <= n_i <= 1000). On each turn, a player chooses ONE heap and splits it into two NON-EMPTY heaps of DIFFERENT sizes (a split into two equal halves is illegal). The player who cannot make any move (every heap has size 0, 1, or 2, none of which can be legally split) loses. Determine the winner under optimal play: print "First" or "Second".
examples.approach: First compute the Grundy number g[n] for a single heap of size n, for n = 0..1000, via g[n] = mex over all splits (a, b) with a + b = n, a != b, a,b >= 1, of (g[a] XOR g[b]) — the XOR appears because after splitting, the heap becomes two INDEPENDENT heaps, and Sprague-Grundy says their combined Grundy value is the XOR of the two. g[0] = g[1] = g[2] = 0 (no legal split exists, mex of empty set is 0). Once the table is built, the overall game is the disjunctive sum of the m given heaps, so its Grundy number is the XOR of g[n_1], g[n_2], ..., g[n_m]; the first player wins iff this XOR is nonzero.

examples.title: Nim with a Restricted Move Set (Subtraction Game)
examples.problem: There are m independent piles (1 <= m <= 1000), the i-th pile having n_i stones (0 <= n_i <= 1000). On each turn, a player chooses a nonempty pile and removes EXACTLY 1, 3, or 4 stones from it (removing any other amount is illegal, and if a pile has fewer than 1 stone no move is possible on it, but if it has 2 stones only the 'remove 1' option applies since removing 3 or 4 is impossible). The player who cannot move (every pile has 0 stones) loses. Determine the winner under optimal play: print "First" or "Second".
examples.approach: Because the allowed removals are restricted, plain Nim's 'XOR the pile sizes' rule does NOT apply directly — you must first compute each pile's Grundy number under this specific move set. Build a table g[0..1000] where g[0] = 0 and g[n] = mex({ g[n-1], g[n-3], g[n-4] } intersected with valid indices >= 0). This sequence turns out to be periodic with period 7 (0,1,0,1,2,3,2, repeating), but the DP computes it correctly without needing to notice that. Once every pile's Grundy number is known, XOR them all together (this is valid because the piles are independent subgames); the first player wins iff the XOR is nonzero.

examples.title: Composite Game with Heterogeneous Pile Types
examples.problem: There are m independent piles (1 <= m <= 1000), each of one of three TYPES, given as a type letter and a size: type 'A' piles allow removing 1 or 2 stones per move; type 'B' piles allow removing exactly 1, 3, or 4 stones per move; type 'C' piles are standard Nim piles where any positive number of stones may be removed. On each turn, a player picks any one nonempty pile (of any type) and makes a legal move on it according to ITS OWN type's rule. The player who cannot move (every pile is empty) loses. Determine the winner under optimal play: print "First" or "Second".
examples.approach: This is a genuine composite game made of three DIFFERENT kinds of subgames. Sprague-Grundy still applies: compute each pile's Grundy number using the rule for ITS type, independent of the other piles. For type A (subtraction {1,2}), a short hand-derivation (or a DP) shows g_A(n) = n mod 3. For type B (subtraction {1,3,4}), use the same mex-DP as before. For type C (standard Nim pile), g_C(n) = n exactly (a pile of n stones can move to any smaller pile 0..n-1, so mex({0,...,n-1}) = n). Compute each given pile's Grundy number by dispatching on its type, then XOR ALL of them together across the whole composite game; the first player wins iff the total XOR is nonzero. This demonstrates the full generality of Sprague-Grundy: it doesn't matter that the subgames are structurally different from each other, only that each is independent and impartial.
